sort-list.pattern: Divide and conquer: merge sort on a linked list (split at the middle, sort halves, merge)

approaches.name: Insertion sort by relinking
approaches.idea: Build a sorted list one node at a time: take each node from the input and walk the sorted list to find where it belongs.
steps: Start with an empty sorted list behind a dummy head.
For each node in the input, walk from the dummy until the next node is larger, and splice the node in there.
approaches.why: Each insertion may walk the whole sorted list, so 5 × 10⁴ nodes means about 10⁹ steps in the worst case. Correct, but too slow for the performance test.

approaches.name: Copy values to an array and sort
approaches.idea: Read the values into an array, sort it with the library sort, and write the sorted values back into the nodes in order.
steps: Walk the list and collect every value.
Sort the array.
Walk the list again, overwriting each node's value with the next sorted value.
approaches.why: Fast and simple, and often acceptable in practice. It misses the follow-up (O(1) extra memory), and it changes node values instead of relinking nodes, which an interviewer may disallow.

approaches.name: Merge sort: split with slow/fast pointers, merge by relinking
approaches.idea: Divide: find the middle with slow and fast pointers and cut the list in two. Conquer: sort each half recursively. Combine: merge two sorted lists by relinking nodes behind a dummy head.
steps: A list of 0 or 1 nodes is sorted.
Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps (starting `fast` at `head.next`) so `slow` stops at the end of the first half; cut after it.
Sort both halves recursively.
Merge: repeatedly attach the smaller head to the tail of the result, then append whatever remains.
approaches.why: log n levels of splitting, O(n) merging per level. The only extra memory is the recursion stack. For strictly O(1) space, run merge sort bottom-up: merge adjacent runs of length 1, then 2, 4, … iteratively.

different-ways-to-add-parentheses.pattern: Divide and conquer on the last operator applied, with memoisation

approaches.name: Split at every operator, recursively
approaches.idea: Any full parenthesisation applies some operator last. For each operator, compute every result of the left side and every result of the right side, then combine each pair. A string with no operator is a number.
steps: For each operator at index i: left = all results of expression[0..i), right = all results of expression(i..].
Add `a op b` for every a in left and b in right.
If no operator was found, return the number itself.
approaches.why: Cₙ is the n-th Catalan number, the count of groupings for n operators; the answer itself has that many values, so no algorithm can beat its size. Without memoisation, the same sub-expressions are recomputed under many different splits.

approaches.name: Same split, memoised by substring
approaches.idea: The recursion asks for the same sub-expressions over and over (for example the middle part of a long expression). Cache each substring's list of results so each is computed once.
steps: Before computing a substring, return its cached list if present.
Otherwise split at each operator as before, combine the results, and cache the list.
approaches.why: There are only O(n²) distinct substrings, so repeated work disappears; the remaining cost is producing the answer itself, which has Catalan-many values. Memoising on (start, end) indices instead of substrings avoids building strings.

longest-substring-with-at-least-k-repeat.pattern: Divide and conquer: split the string at characters that can never be in a valid substring

approaches.name: Check every substring with running counts
approaches.idea: Fix each start, extend the end one character at a time keeping counts, and after each step check whether every present character has count at least k.
steps: For each start i, reset a 26-entry count array.
For each end j ≥ i: add s[j], then check the counts; if valid, update the best length.
approaches.why: n² substrings with a 26-step check each: about 2.6 × 10⁹ operations at n = 10⁴, too slow for the performance test.

approaches.name: Sliding window per number of distinct letters
approaches.idea: A plain sliding window fails because adding characters can both break and restore validity. Fix the number of distinct letters u (1 to 26): for each u, a window with at most u distinct letters is monotone, and it is valid when exactly u letters each reach k.
steps: For u = 1 … 26: slide a window keeping counts, the number of distinct letters, and how many letters have count ≥ k.
Grow the right end; shrink from the left while distinct > u.
If distinct == u and all u letters have count ≥ k, record the window length.
approaches.why: Each of the 26 passes moves both pointers at most n times. A good alternative when the interviewer wants an iterative solution; the divide-and-conquer version below is easier to come up with.

approaches.name: Divide and conquer on the "bad" characters
approaches.idea: Count letters in the current range. A letter appearing fewer than k times can't be in any valid substring, so split the range at every such letter and solve each piece; a range with no such letter is valid as a whole.
steps: If the range is shorter than k, return 0.
Count each letter in the range.
If every present letter has count ≥ k, return the range length.
Otherwise split at each letter with count < k and return the best answer among the pieces.
approaches.why: Each recursion level does O(n) total counting across its pieces, and every level removes at least one of the 26 letters from consideration, so the depth is at most 26. Splitting at every bad letter at once (not just the first) keeps the recursion shallow.
